newsitem.title: FRANCE: Algerian leaders strike pact at disputed conference.
newsitem.headline: Algerian leaders strike pact at disputed conference.

text.p: Thirty-eight Algerian party, union and other leaders signed a pact on Sunday at the end of a disputed national conference to pave the way for a multi-party system and general elections next year.

President Liamine Zeroual was shown live on Algerian state television applauding the 37 men and one woman who signed at the conference boycotted by two main secular parties and from which radical Islamists were barred.
The pact aims to end nearly five years of violence, blamed on fundamentalists, in which some 50,000 people have died.
Zeroual, who chaired the conference, did not sign the pact -- a signal displaying him as a leader above the fractious political scene.

Outside the seaside complex of Palais des Nations, 25 km (12 miles) from Algiers, where 1,000 politicians gathered at the National Conference of Understanding, politicians and analysts questionned the impact of the conference.
Some said they doubted whether the pact would end violence, reunite the country and end political conflict.
The conference, at least in the short term, failed to alter the indifference of Algiers residents.

"We have heard of talks to resolve the crisis so many times before," said one resident summing up the mood of a population tired by killings, economic hardship and the endless squabbles of politicians.
Main opposition parties stayed away, with one accusing Zeroual of trying to forge an "anti-Islamist front" rather than seek a peaceful solution.

Their absence could well undermine the conference which took into the limelight mainly unknown politicians to sign the pact dubbed a milestone in Zeroual's drive to forge consensus on his planned reforms.

Many are seen as lacking strong grassroots support except for the legal Islamist Hamas leader Mahfoud Nahnah, who took more than 2.9 million votes in last year's presidential poll, and Boualem Benhamouda, head of the former ruling National Liberation Front (FLN).
The main workers' union leader Abdelhaq Benhamouda and the chief of the former liberation war fighters movement, Mohamed Cherif Abbas also signed, with an array of small social and political groups.

The pact bans use of Islam, Arabic and Berber languages as political weapons to win power, condemns violence and lays the framework for a multi-party democracy. It also confirms Zeroual's political agenda to hold a referendum to amend the constitution and general and local elections next year.

"The final text of the (pact) platform...will have no impact in a balanced evolution of the society because of lack of thorough debate and the lack of maturity in its solutions", said former prime minister Mouloud Hamrouche.
Hamrouche, a leading figure in the FLN, in a letter to Zeroual which was published on Sunday, added:

"Therefore, the urgent question should be raised whether the platform as a conclusion to the conference will help end marginalistion and division, erase feeling of injustice and hatred and spur a social and political mobilisation."

"Without political partners representing various trends of ideas and thinking about another Algeria, it would be political blindness to say the conference will reach its goal to build a national understanding. There was no national understanding there", a leading Algerian newspaper Liberte said on Sunday.
Zeroual denied the country's politicians were divided and that the Algerian people were indifferent to the government.
"Your debates were refutation of those allegations about divisiveness in the country," Zeroual was shown telling the conference on Sunday on state-run television.
